t: The agricultural year in India, used for crop statistics, runs from:
e: The agricultural year (July–June) aligns with the start of the kharif sowing season, unlike the financial year used for budgets and insurance accounts.

t: What is the approximate share of agriculture and allied activities in India's total Gross Value Added in recent years?
e: Agriculture and allied sectors contribute roughly 18% of GVA while still engaging around 45% of the workforce, a mismatch that underlines low farm incomes and the need for risk protection.

t: Crop insurance is a technique of:
e: Insurance transfers the financial consequence of a loss to an insurer in exchange for premium; it does not prevent the loss (avoidance/elimination) nor does the farmer bear it himself (retention).

topic: History of Crop Insurance in India
t: Under NAIS, the indemnity levels available were:
e: NAIS used 60% (high risk), 80% (medium risk) and 90% (low risk) indemnity levels. PMFBY raised the lowest level to 70%.

topic: History of Crop Insurance in India
t: Under NAIS, the threshold yield for rice and wheat was based on a moving average of the yield of the preceding:
e: NAIS used a 3-year moving average for rice and wheat and a 5-year moving average for other crops. PMFBY uses the best 5 of 7 years for all crops.

topic: History of Crop Insurance in India
t: The Farm Income Insurance Scheme (FIIS) piloted in 2003–04 was distinctive because it:
o: Protected against shortfall in income by covering both yield loss and price fall below the Minimum Support Price
Was implemented by private insurers only
e: FIIS, piloted by AIC for wheat and rice in selected districts, guaranteed income (yield × MSP); it was discontinued after 2004–05 and India returned to yield-based cover.

topic: History of Crop Insurance in India
t: The Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme (WBCIS) was first piloted in India in:
e: AIC piloted WBCIS in Kharif 2007 in Karnataka after earlier rainfall insurance experiments (Varsha Bima, 2004). It was restructured as RWBCIS in 2016.

t: A feature of crop insurance design intended to reduce the time lag in claim payment under the area approach is:
o: Increasing the size of the insurance unit
Requiring the farmer to submit a loss survey report
On-account (interim) payment during the season based on expected yield shortfall
e: Because area-yield claims await CCE results after harvest, PMFBY provides on-account payments (25% of likely claims) for mid-season adversity to give farmers immediate relief.

t: Which of the following is a reason why pure private, unsubsidised multi-peril crop insurance has rarely succeeded anywhere in the world?
o: Farmers are legally barred from buying private insurance
Reinsurers refuse to cover any agricultural risk
Systemic risk, high administrative cost and adverse selection make actuarially fair premiums unaffordable for most farmers
Crop losses never occur in developed countries
e: Multi-peril crop insurance everywhere (USA, Canada, Spain, India, China) depends on premium subsidy and public reinsurance support because correlated losses and information problems push unsubsidised premiums beyond farmers' willingness to pay.

t: The Fund for Innovation and Technology (FIAT) created under PMFBY in 2025 is intended to:
o: Finance technology initiatives such as YES-TECH and WINDS and research for improving the scheme
Compensate insurers for losses above the cap
Set up a new public sector crop insurer
e: The Cabinet in January 2025 approved continuation of PMFBY/RWBCIS up to 2025–26 and a FIAT corpus of about ₹825 crore for technology (yield estimation, weather data networks) and R&D.

t: In a stop loss treaty on a crop portfolio written as '100% of 110% in excess of 110% of premium', the reinsurer will pay losses:
o: Up to a 110% loss ratio only
Above a 110% loss ratio up to a 220% loss ratio
Above a 220% loss ratio without limit
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). The cedant retains losses up to 110% of premium; the reinsurer covers the next 110% (i.e. loss ratios from 110% to 220%). Losses beyond 220% fall back on the cedant unless further layers are bought.

topic: Crop Insurance - Yield Index based Underwriting and Claims
t: The technology-based yield estimation system integrated into PMFBY, using remote sensing to estimate yield with a minimum 30% weightage, is called:
e: YES-TECH (Yield Estimation System based on Technology) blends remote-sensing yield estimates with CCE data. WINDS is the weather station network, CROPIC collects crop photographs and AIDE is the intermediary enrolment app.

topic: Crop Insurance - Yield Index based Underwriting and Claims
t: The WINDS initiative under PMFBY aims to:
o: Provide crop loans to insured farmers
Set up automatic weather stations and rain gauges at block and gram panchayat level to create hyper-local weather data
e: WINDS (Weather Information Network Data Systems) expands the AWS/ARG network five-fold to provide dense, reliable weather data for RWBCIS and for adverse-weather provisions of PMFBY.

topic: Crop Insurance - Yield Index based Underwriting and Claims
t: Under PMFBY, the cut-off date for enrolment of farmers for Kharif crops is generally:
e: The standard enrolment cut-off is 31 July for Kharif and 31 December for Rabi, with the State notification able to vary it for specific crops. Banks must upload loanee data by the cut-off.

topic: Crop Insurance - Yield Index based Underwriting and Claims
t: Under PMFBY, the Insurance Unit for major crops is the:
e: For major crops the IU is the village or village panchayat; for other crops it may be a larger unit such as the block/taluka, as notified by the State.

topic: Crop Insurance - Yield Index based Underwriting and Claims
t: In an Insurance Unit, the yields for the past seven years (kg/ha) are 1,800, 2,100, 1,200, 2,000, 1,900, 2,200 and 1,000. With an indemnity level of 80%, the Threshold Yield under PMFBY is:
e: Best 5 of 7 = 2,200 + 2,100 + 2,000 + 1,900 + 1,800 = 10,000; average = 2,000 kg/ha. TY = 80% × 2,000 = 1,600 kg/ha. Using all seven years (average 1,743) would be wrong.

topic: Crop Insurance - Yield Index based Underwriting and Claims
t: Under PMFBY, a non-loanee farmer must furnish which of the following at the time of enrolment?
o: A loan sanction letter from the bank
Land records (or tenancy/sharecropping proof), sowing certificate or self-declaration, bank account details and Aadhaar
e: Non-loanee farmers enrol through banks, CSCs, intermediaries or the portal with land records/tenancy proof, crop sowing details and bank/Aadhaar particulars for direct benefit transfer of claims.

topic: Traditional Crop Insurance: Underwriting and Claims
t: In a named-peril individual crop policy, a 'franchise' of 10% means:
o: Losses below 10% of the sum insured are not paid, but once the loss exceeds 10% it is paid in full
10% of every loss is deducted from each claim
The farmer must pay 10% of the premium
Cover is restricted to 10% of the crop area
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). A franchise is a threshold: below it nothing is payable, above it the whole loss is payable. A deductible (excess), in contrast, is subtracted from every claim.

topic: Crop Insurance - Yield Index based Underwriting and Claims
t: The DigiClaim module of PMFBY introduced in 2023 enables:
o: Automatic enrolment of all land owners
Direct transfer of claim amounts to farmers' bank accounts through the National Crop Insurance Portal linked to PFMS
Online purchase of reinsurance by insurers
e: DigiClaim automates claim computation and disbursal through the NCIP and the Public Financial Management System, improving transparency and speed of settlement to farmers.

topic: Crop Insurance - Yield Index based Underwriting and Claims
t: Which statement about the Crop Insurance App (and the AIDE/Sahayak app) under PMFBY is correct?
o: The app is available only to bank managers
Farmers can enrol, check policy status and intimate localised crop loss within 72 hours through the app
The app replaces the need for crop cutting experiments
The app is used to pay premium subsidy to insurers
e: The Crop Insurance App allows farmer enrolment, status tracking and crop-loss intimation; AIDE lets intermediaries enrol non-loanee farmers at the doorstep. CCEs continue for yield estimation.

t: Which type of crop is generally more suited to RWBCIS than to PMFBY?
o: Horticultural and perennial crops for which reliable historical yield data from CCEs are not available
Paddy in irrigated areas with long yield history
Crops grown only under contract farming
e: Where yield series are inadequate for actuarial pricing, weather indices correlated with crop performance (rainfall, temperature) are used; hence RWBCIS is common for mango, grapes, chilli, potato and spices.

t: Under RWBCIS, an 'Automatic Weather Station' differs from a manual rain gauge in that it:
o: Records rainfall only once a month
Records multiple parameters (rainfall, temperature, humidity, wind) at frequent intervals and transmits data electronically
e: AWS equipment provides tamper-proof, time-stamped multi-parameter data needed for weather indices; Automatic Rain Gauges (ARGs) record rainfall only.

t: In a weather-index term sheet, a 'consecutive dry days' index is designed to capture:
o: Total rainfall for the entire season
Prolonged dry spells within the season that damage the crop even when total seasonal rainfall is normal
e: Crop damage often depends on the distribution of rainfall, so CDD indices pay when the number of consecutive days with rainfall below a threshold exceeds a trigger, complementing cumulative deficit indices.

t: The weather data provider for RWBCIS claim settlement must be:
o: IMD or an agency approved/notified by the State Government, independent of the insurer
e: Data for settlement must come from IMD stations or notified third-party AWS providers accredited by the State, so that both farmers and insurers can rely on the objectivity of the index.

t: A term sheet pays ₹500 per °C for each day on which the maximum temperature exceeds 40°C during a 15-day phase, with a maximum of ₹10,000 per hectare. Records show maximum temperatures of 42°C, 41°C and 43°C on three days and below 40°C on all other days. The payout is:
e: Excess degrees = 2 + 1 + 3 = 6°C × ₹500 = ₹3,000, which is within the ₹10,000 maximum.

topic: Traditional Crop Insurance: Underwriting and Claims
t: Under an individual-approach plantation policy, 'loss of trees' is commonly indemnified by:
o: Paying the full sum insured whenever any tree is damaged
Paying the market value of the harvested produce
Paying the age-based value per tree as per the valuation schedule for trees destroyed by an insured peril
e: Plantation policies (rubber, tea, coconut, arecanut, oil palm) value trees by age and pay for trees lost to fire, flood, storm, pests, etc., less any excess.

topic: Traditional Crop Insurance: Underwriting and Claims
t: A grape grower insures 2 hectares against hailstorm with a sum insured of ₹3 lakh per hectare, subject to an excess of 10% of the sum insured on each claim. A hailstorm causes 50% damage on the whole area. The claim payable is:
e: Loss = 50% × ₹6,00,000 = ₹3,00,000. Excess = 10% × ₹6,00,000 = ₹60,000. Net claim = ₹3,00,000 − ₹60,000 = ₹2,40,000. Deducting 10% of the loss (₹30,000) instead of 10% of sum insured would give the wrong figure ₹2,70,000.

t: The Unified Package Insurance Scheme (UPIS) launched in 2016 requires a farmer to take crop insurance plus at least how many other sections?
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). UPIS bundles seven covers: crop (PMFBY/RWBCIS), building and contents, agricultural implements, tractor, pump set, personal accident and student safety, with life (PMJJBY) also available. Crop cover plus at least two other sections is mandatory.

topic: Traditional Crop Insurance: Underwriting and Claims
t: Which crop is traditionally insured in India on an individual, named-peril basis rather than under area-yield index schemes?
e: Field crops with wide coverage and yield data (paddy, wheat, bajra) are under PMFBY; plantation crops such as rubber, tea, coffee and cardamom are covered through individual named-peril policies offered by insurers.

t: Index-Based Livestock Insurance (IBLI), which pays herders on the basis of satellite-measured pasture conditions (NDVI), was pioneered in:
e: IBLI, developed by ILRI for pastoralists in northern Kenya (2010) and Ethiopia, uses NDVI forage indices to predict livestock mortality; Mongolia runs a similar index-based livestock scheme on mortality rates.

t: In the United States, 'Revenue Protection' crop insurance differs from yield protection because it:
o: Is sold only to livestock farmers
Guarantees revenue by covering both yield shortfall and a decline in the harvest price relative to the projected price
e: Revenue Protection, the most popular US product, uses futures prices at planting and harvest to guarantee revenue, whereas Yield Protection indemnifies only bushel shortfall at the projected price.

topic: Livestock / Cattle Wealth in Indian Economy
t: Which of the following best describes the importance of livestock for small and marginal farmers in India?
o: Livestock is owned only by large farmers
Livestock contributes nothing to household income
Livestock provides a steady supplementary income and acts as a buffer against crop failure
Livestock is maintained solely for religious reasons
e: Over 80% of livestock is owned by small, marginal and landless households, giving daily cash flow from milk and eggs; this is why livestock insurance has strong welfare value.

topic: Livestock / Cattle Wealth in Indian Economy
t: India ranks first in the world in population of:
e: India has the world's largest buffalo population (over 100 million, roughly 55% of the world total) and the largest cattle population; it ranks second in goats.

t: Which exotic dairy breed, originating from the Channel Islands, is widely used in India for crossbreeding because of its adaptability and high fat milk?
e: Jersey is a small-bodied breed with high-fat milk and better heat tolerance than Holstein Friesian, making it the preferred exotic breed for crossbreeding in many Indian states. Hereford is a beef breed.

t: The 'lactation period' of a dairy cow refers to:
o: The gestation period of about 280 days
The period during which the cow produces milk after calving, normally about 300 days
e: Milk yield per lactation (about 300 days) and the number of lactations completed determine an animal's market value and therefore its sum insured; the dry period follows before the next calving.

t: Since 1 April 2021, the standard fire policy for a dwelling in India is:
o: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Bharat Griha Raksha for homes; Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha (up to ₹5 crore) and Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha (₹5–50 crore) for enterprises.

t: Which of the following perils is covered under the standard cattle insurance policy?
o: Death due to flood, cyclone or earthquake
Death due to war or nuclear perils
e: Cattle cover includes death by accident (including natural calamities), disease and surgery. Theft, clandestine sale, war and nuclear risks are excluded.

t: The age of an animal proposed for cattle insurance is generally determined by:
o: Dentition (examination of the teeth) by the veterinary doctor
e: Dentition gives a reliable estimate of age; the vet records age, breed, colour, identification marks, milk yield and market value in the health certificate.

t: Under cattle insurance, when an insured animal is sold during the policy period, the policy:
o: Is transferable to the new owner only with the insurer's consent and endorsement
Automatically continues in favour of the buyer
Stands cancelled with full refund of premium
Covers the buyer and the seller jointly
e: Insurable interest must exist at the time of loss; on sale, the insurer must be informed and the policy endorsed in favour of the buyer, failing which no claim is payable.

t: A dairy farmer insures 4 buffaloes for ₹80,000 each at a premium rate of 4% under a one-year policy with PTD extension at an additional 1%. The total premium payable is:
e: Total sum insured = 4 × ₹80,000 = ₹3,20,000. Rate = 4% + 1% = 5%. Premium = 5% × ₹3,20,000 = ₹16,000 (plus GST as applicable).

t: A claim is lodged for an insured cow that died on the 10th day after inception of the policy from a bacterial disease. The claim will be:
o: Repudiated, since death due to disease within 15 days of inception is excluded
Paid only if the owner produces a police report
e: The 15-day waiting period for disease deaths applies unless the policy is a renewal in continuity. Only accidental deaths are covered from inception.

t: Under poultry insurance the minimum flock size generally insured is of the order of:
o: A few hundred birds (e.g. 500 broilers or 200 layers), as per insurer's norms
e: Poultry cover is written for commercial farms with reasonable flock sizes so that the standard-mortality excess works meaningfully; individual backyard birds are not insured.

t: Under Section 45 of the Insurance Act 1938, a life insurance policy cannot be called in question on any ground after how many years from the date of issue, revival or rider addition, whichever is later?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). The 2015 amendment made the three-year bar absolute: after three years no policy may be questioned on any ground, including fraud.

t: For layer birds, the valuation per bird under the poultry policy generally reaches its peak at:
o: About 20 weeks (point of lay) and thereafter declines
e: Rearing cost accumulates until the pullet starts laying (around 18–20 weeks); afterwards the bird's residual value declines as the laying life remaining falls.

t: A broiler farmer insures 5,000 birds. The policy fixes standard mortality at 5% and values birds at ₹120 each in the relevant week. A disease outbreak kills 650 birds. The claim payable is:
e: Standard mortality = 5% × 5,000 = 250 birds. Excess deaths = 650 − 250 = 400 × ₹120 = ₹48,000, subject to the policy's other conditions.

t: Under the Coconut Palm Insurance Scheme, palms are insurable in the age group of:
e: CPIS covers healthy, bearing palms from 4 (dwarf) or 7 (tall) years up to 60 years against death/loss due to storm, flood, fire, lightning, pests, diseases and other listed perils.

t: Brackish water shrimp (prawn) culture insurance in India typically indemnifies:
o: Total loss of the stocked crop in a pond due to covered perils, with sum insured based on a percentage (around 80%) of input cost
Fall in export price of shrimp
e: Shrimp policies are on a total-loss basis for the pond cycle; the sum insured excludes a margin of input cost, and perils such as disease (e.g. white spot), flood, pollution and poisoning are covered subject to conditions.

t: Which of the following animals can be insured under miscellaneous livestock policies offered by Indian insurers?
o: Camel, horse, elephant, pig and pet dog
e: Besides cattle, insurers offer policies for horses/ponies/donkeys, camels, elephants, pigs, rabbits, ducks, dogs and honey bees, each with its own age limits, valuation and exclusions.

t: The main reason crop insurers in India depend heavily on international reinsurers is:
o: IRDAI prohibits retention of crop risk
Crop insurance has no risk at all
Farmers pay premium directly to reinsurers
The catastrophic, highly correlated nature of crop losses which a single insurer's capital cannot absorb in a bad monsoon year
e: A widespread drought can produce loss ratios of several hundred percent in a cluster; reinsurance (stop loss, quota share) spreads this across the global market. Retention is permitted but capital-constrained.

t: 'Retrocession' means:
o: Return of premium to the farmer
Reinsurance purchased by a reinsurer to protect its own accepted portfolio
The State's share of premium subsidy
e: A reinsurer that has accepted large crop exposures may in turn cede part of them to other reinsurers; this reinsurance of reinsurance is called retrocession.
